title: Quantum Charge as a Particle/Antiparticle Label
abstract: We show that the concept of particles and antiparticles is related to the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$. Its generators are the position operators $\hat x^a$, the momentum operators $\hat p_a$, and the central element $Q_{\sf{v}}$, which defines a subgroup U(1)$_{\sf v}$ of $W\!H_3$. We show that the wave functions have a charge relative to the group U(1)$_{\sf{v}}$ equal to either $q_+=1/\hbar$ (particle $ψ_+$) or $q_-=-1/\hbar$ (antiparticle $ψ_-$). We call these eigenvalues of the operator $Q_{\sf{v}}$ quantum charges: $Q_{\sf{v}}ψ_\pm^{}=q_\pm^{}ψ_\pm^{}$. The wave functions $ψ_+$ and $ψ_-$ belong to the Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_+$ and $\mathcal{H}_-$, on which unitarily inequivalent representations $π_\hbar$ and $π_{-\hbar}$ of the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$ are defined. These representations are related to each other by the antilinear charge conjugation operator $\hat C$, which maps $\mathcal{H}_+, q_+$ to $\mathcal{H}_-, q_-$. Charges $q_\pm^{}$ are intrinsic characteristics of the wave functions $ψ_\pm^{}$, similar to spin and electric charge. The wave function possesses one of these charges, $q_+$ or $q_-$, prior to the specification of any equations. We show that negative probabilities/energies and the Klein paradox in Klein-Gordon and Dirac theories are consequences of the violation of U(1)$_{\sf v}$-invariance in these theories. Restoring this invariance separates particle and antiparticles and eliminates all paradoxes at the level of first-quantized relativistic theories.
summary: This theoretical paper reinterprets particle/antiparticle duality by grounding it in the symmetry structure of the Weyl-Heisenberg group. It shows that defining wave functions with intrinsic 'quantum charges' ($q_\pm$) and enforcing $	ext{U}(1)_v$-invariance is the mathematical requirement needed to eliminate paradoxes found in standard relativistic quantum theories.
main_problem: The paper aims to fundamentally relate the concept of particles and antiparticles to the mathematical structure of the Weyl-Heisenberg group ($	ext{WH}_3$) and show that restoring a specific symmetry eliminates paradoxes in relativistic quantum theories.
main_result: The existence of distinct, unitarily inequivalent Hilbert spaces ($\mathcal{H}_+$ and $\mathcal{H}_-$), labeled by intrinsic 'quantum charges' ($q_+$ and $q_-$), is necessary to maintain $	ext{U}(1)_v$-invariance and resolve issues like the Klein paradox.
method: The analysis uses advanced mathematical tools, including principal bundles, complex line bundles, and the representation theory of the Weyl-Heisenberg group, to impose symmetry constraints on quantum field descriptions.
model_or_system: The model is a theoretical framework applied to relativistic quantum mechanics, specifically analyzing free scalar (Klein-Gordon) and spinor (Dirac) fields. The underlying mathematical structure is the $	ext{U}(1)_v$-bundle over the phase space $\mathbb{R}^6$.
key_observables: Quantum charges ($q_\pm$), electric charges ($e_\pm$), energy ($E$), and the wave functions ($\psi_+, \psi_-$) themselves.
important_parameters: The fundamental constants $\hbar$ and the symmetry charges $q_\pm = \pm 1/\hbar$. The analysis also considers the non-relativistic limit ($c 	o \infty$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the physical description must be invariant under the $	ext{U}(1)_v$ symmetry group to be physically consistent.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the $	ext{WH}_3$ framework and the concept of intrinsic quantum charge ($q_\pm$) to analyzing how this structure dictates the form of relativistic wave equations (Klein-Gordon/Dirac). It then demonstrates that maintaining $	ext{U}(1)_v$-invariance separates particle and antiparticle descriptions, resolving paradoxes.
why_interesting: While not directly focused on AMO systems, the rigorous mathematical treatment of symmetry constraints and the separation of particle/antiparticle states based on fundamental group theory is highly relevant to understanding topological aspects of quantum matter and gauge theories.
